title: Renoviction response and housing supply discussion
subtitle: Also covered: transit electrification audit, second quarter budget adjustments, and the growth management monitoring report on approved but unbuilt housing.
overview: The committee spent most of its meeting on renovictions, where tenants are asked to leave for renovations. After hearing from several delegates, it recommended that staff immediately create an eviction survey and a "Renting in Guelph" web page {{vote:m3}}. It also recommended deferring the five remaining renoviction by-law recommendations to October 8, 2024, when the Housing Affordability Strategy goes to Council {{vote:m4}}.
The committee also received the Transit Electrification Audit for information {{vote:m1}}. It recommended approving the budget adjustments in the second quarter monitoring report {{vote:m2}}.

The Guelph Growth Management and Affordable Housing Monitoring Report was discussed without a motion. Staff agreed to consider more detail on constrained sites and to bring the report forward to Council in future. For residents, the survey and web page are the first concrete steps on evictions. Staff said the work is not yet on their plan and gave no timeline, and Council still has to adopt these recommendations.

decisions.item: Eviction survey and renter landing page
decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff immediately create an eviction survey and a "Renting in Guelph" landing page on tenant rights and resources {{vote:m3}}.
The committee recommended deferring discussion of recommendations 1 to 5 on renoviction by-laws until the Housing Affordability Strategy goes to Council on October 8, 2024 {{vote:m4}}.
The committee recommended approving the adjustments in Tables 4, 5 and 6 of Attachment 2 of the 2024 second quarter budget monitoring report {{vote:m2}}.
The committee received the audit report for information {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Delegates described tenants in Brant-area buildings receiving renovation eviction notices and being told they would not return. They raised short-notice demands, unanswered maintenance requests and seniors who did not know their rights. They asked for fines that actually deter, more transparency from landlords and a landlord registry.

Advocates urged a renovation by-law and landlord licensing, and said administrative costs are small next to the cost of homelessness. One councillor and staff noted that much of the issue sits with the province, and that municipal by-laws are compliance tools.

Councillors asked whether the web page alone would reach tenants without internet skills. They also noted staff had no capacity identified for the new work, and the mover clarified that the items would start immediately but not be ready by October 8.

On the growth report, a development industry delegate said the roughly 6,000 units of short-term supply are heavily constrained by holding provisions, contamination, litigation and financing, and asked for a "shovel ready" measure. Councillors asked what the industry is doing to move stalled sites and asked it to explain its challenges publicly.

Staff said shovel-ready status is hard to track because site plan approval is a moment in time. They said the city does not control financing or the rents charged outside funded programs. In the budget discussion, staff said the cancelled downtown pedestrian bridge project may be revisited in the Macdonald bridge environmental assessment.
